chapter_title: Mastering Blueprint Interfaces for Decoupled Communication
chapter_summary:
As you build more complex games in Unreal Engine, you'll inevitably encounter situations where different Blueprints need to communicate with each other. While direct casting (e.g., `Cast To PlayerCharacter`) is a common initial approach, it quickly leads to tight coupling – meaning one Blueprint directly depends on the specific type of another. This makes your code harder to maintain, extend, and debug. Imagine having twenty different types of interactable objects (doors, levers, pickups, NPCs) that all need to respond to a player's "Interact" action. If you used casting, your player character would need a long chain of `Cast To` nodes, one for each interactable type, which is inefficient and brittle. This is where Blueprint Interfaces shine.

Blueprint Interfaces provide a powerful solution by defining a "contract" that any Blueprint can choose to implement. Think of it like a universal remote control. The remote doesn't care if it's controlling a Sony TV or a Samsung TV, as long as both TVs understand the "Power On" signal. Similarly, an interface defines a set of functions (called "messages") that a Blueprint *can* respond to, without the calling Blueprint needing to know the specific class of the target. When you call an interface message, Unreal Engine checks if the target object implements that interface. If it does, the corresponding function in the target object is executed. If not, nothing happens, and no errors occur. This "don't care what you are, just respond if you can" approach is the essence of decoupled communication.

To create a Blueprint Interface, you'll navigate to the Content Browser, right-click, and select `Blueprints -> Blueprint Interface`. Once created, you can open it and add functions, which will become your "messages." These functions can have inputs and outputs, just like regular functions, but they have no implementation details within the interface itself. They are purely declarations. For example, you might create an interface named `BPI_Interactable` with a single function `Interact` that takes a `PlayerController` reference as an input.

Implementing an interface on an Actor or Component Blueprint is straightforward. Open the target Blueprint, go to the `Class Settings` (or `Details` panel for Components), and under the `Interfaces` section, click `Add` and select your `BPI_Interactable`. Once added, you'll see the interface functions appear in the `My Blueprint` panel under a new `Interfaces` category. You can then right-click on an interface function (e.g., `Interact`) and select `Implement Event` or `Implement Function`. This creates the actual logic for how *this specific Blueprint* responds to that message. For a door, `Interact` might open it. For a pickup, `Interact` might add it to the player's inventory.

Calling an interface message is equally simple. When you have a reference to an Actor or Component that *might* implement your interface, you can drag off its pin and search for the interface message function (e.g., `Interact (Message)`). Crucially, before calling the message, it's good practice to use the `Does Implement Interface` node. This node takes an object reference and an interface class, returning true if the object implements that interface. This check ensures that you only attempt to send messages to objects that are capable of responding, preventing unnecessary processing and making your logic clearer. A common mistake is to forget this check, leading to messages being sent to objects that ignore them, which can be hard to debug if you expect a specific behavior.

Consider a scenario where your player character needs to interact with various objects in the world. Instead of casting to `BP_Door`, then `BP_Lever`, then `BP_Pickup`, and so on, your player character only needs to know about `BPI_Interactable`. When the player presses the interact key, you perform a line trace or sphere overlap to find objects in front of them. For each hit object, you use `Does Implement Interface (BPI_Interactable)`. If true, you then call `Interact (Message)` on that object, passing the player character's reference. Each interactable object then handles its own unique interaction logic. This design significantly reduces dependencies, makes it easy to add new interactable types without modifying the player character, and promotes modularity.

Another key advantage of interfaces over direct casting is that they work across different inheritance hierarchies. You can have a `BP_Door` (inheriting from `Actor`) and a `BP_Switch` (inheriting from `Actor`) and a `BP_InventoryComponent` (inheriting from `ActorComponent`) all implement the same `BPI_Interactable` interface. Your calling Blueprint doesn't care about their base class, only that they adhere to the interface contract. This flexibility is invaluable for complex game architectures. While Event Dispatchers also offer decoupled communication, they are primarily for one-to-many broadcasting, where many listeners react to a single event. Interfaces are more suited for one-to-one or one-to-few interactions where you want to invoke a specific action on a specific target object. Choosing between them depends on whether you need to *command* a specific action (interface) or *notify* about an event (dispatcher).

screens.title: Mastering Blueprint Interfaces
screens.subtitle: Design decoupled interactions so Blueprints speak the same language without knowing each other's type.

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn why Blueprint Interfaces are essential for keeping your Blueprints modular and maintainable. Rather than writing many cast chains that force one Blueprint to know another's exact class, an interface defines a contract of messages any object can implement. You'll see how to create an interface asset, implement its message on Actors or Components, call messages safely with a Does Implement Interface check, and choose when interfaces are a better fit than casting or event dispatchers. The hands-on example walks through a light switch: an interface with a ToggleLight message implemented by a BP_Light Actor and called by the player using a sphere overlap. Along the way we'll cover common mistakes and debugging tips so you don't send messages to objects that silently ignore them. By the end, you'll be able to design one-to-one command-style interactions and add new interactable types without changing your player code. Think of the interface as a universal remote: the caller sends a familiar signal, and any object that understands it responds. How will you use that pattern in your current project?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Blueprint Interfaces let objects agree on messages to receive, enabling interaction without tight coupling or repeated casting.

narration.text: These learning objectives map to practical skills you'll use immediately. First, you'll be able to explain what a Blueprint Interface is and why it promotes decoupled communication by defining a message contract rather than a concrete class relationship. Second, you'll create an interface asset and add functions that act as messages, so other Blueprints can opt in to respond. Third, you'll implement interface functions on Actors or Components through Class Settings and add concrete behavior like opening a door or toggling a light. Fourth, you'll call interface messages correctly by checking with Does Implement Interface first, so your logic only attempts messages on objects that can respond. Each objective is framed as an applied skill: after this chapter you won't only know the theory, you'll implement a working interactable and reason about when interfaces beat casting or event dispatchers. That combination of explanation, hands-on creation, and safe invocation prepares you to refactor brittle cast chains into clean, modular interactions.

screens.title: Why casting leads to tight coupling
screens.subtitle: Understand the maintenance cost of many cast chains and when it breaks down

narration.text: Casting is often the first approach when Blueprints need to talk to each other, but it creates a direct dependency: the caller must know the callee's exact class. Imagine a player that must interact with doors, levers, pickups, and NPCs. With casting, the player graph contains a long set of cast nodes—one per possible type—each wiring to its own behavior. That makes adding a new interactable require touching the player, which increases maintenance and introduces regressions. Casting also disregards components or classes outside the expected inheritance tree, so a component that should react to interactions can't be reached without extra plumbing. A common misconception is that casting is simpler because it gives access to specific functions or variables; while true, this convenience couples code tightly. The practical alternative is an interface: the player checks whether the object implements the interface and then calls a generic message. This removes the need to know precise types while preserving the ability to call behavior. Think: do you want the player to command a capability, or to know every possible target class? That distinction guides the choice between casting and interfaces.

keyIdea.title: Casting vs Interfaces
keyIdea.text: Casting ties the caller to concrete types; interfaces decouple the caller from target classes by relying on a shared message contract.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Why casting leads to tight coupling
Why casting leads to tight coupling
Understand the maintenance cost of many cast chains and when it breaks down
Casting pattern (problem)
// Pseudocode representation of many casts
HitResult -> HitActor
-> Cast To BP_Door ? OpenDoor():
-> Cast To BP_Lever ? FlipLever():
-> Cast To BP_Pickup ? AddToInventory():
-> Cast To BP_NPC ? Talk():
// Each new interactable means adding a new cast branch
This code shows how the player must list every class it might interact with. Each branch increases maintenance and breaks the Open/Close principle: adding a new interactable forces a change in the player Blueprint.
Interface pattern (solution)
Does Implement Interface(BPI_Interactable) → Interact(Message)
Here the player only knows BPI_Interactable. Any object implementing that interface receives the Interact message. Adding new interactables does not require edits to the player. The interface acts like a universal remote: a single signal that many device types can respond to in their own way.
Common misconception
Casting is not always wrong; when you need class-specific data or methods not exposed by an interface, cast. But favor interfaces for general commands to reduce coupling and simplify extension.

screens.title: What is a Blueprint Interface?
screens.subtitle: A contract of messages that any Blueprint may implement

narration.text: A Blueprint Interface is a declaration-only asset that lists functions, called messages, which other Blueprints can implement. It contains no implementation details; it only specifies a function name and its inputs and outputs. That declaration becomes a contract: any Blueprint that implements the interface promises it understands and can respond to those messages. For example, a BPI_Interactable might declare Interact with a PlayerController reference as input. A BP_Door could implement that message to open, a BP_Pickup could add itself to inventory, and a BP_Switch could toggle a state. The key benefit is decoupling: the caller sends Interact without needing to know whether the target is a door, pickup, or switch. A common misunderstanding is that interfaces automatically pass state; they don't. They only allow messages. If you need shared data, either expose explicit inputs/outputs on the message or design component APIs. In practice, interfaces let you add new implementers freely, keeping the calling Blueprint unchanged. Reflect: which repeated cast chains in your project could become a simple interface call? What is a Blueprint Interface? means an interface declares messages without implementation, letting diverse blueprints respond in their own way.. In practical terms, a contract of messages that any blueprint may implement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interface = Contract
keyIdea.text: An interface declares messages without implementation, letting diverse Blueprints respond in their own way.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is a Blueprint Interface?
What is a Blueprint Interface?
A contract of messages that any Blueprint may implement
Definition & behavior
  • Contains function declarations only, no implementation.
  • Functions are called messages; they accept inputs and outputs like regular functions.
  • Any Blueprint can implement the interface and supply its own behavior for each message.
Concrete example
Create BPI_Interactable with Interact(PlayerController). BP_Door implements Interact to open; BP_Pickup implements Interact to add itself to inventory. The player only calls Interact and remains agnostic to the target's class.
When interfaces matter
Use interfaces when you want objects from different class hierarchies to respond to the same command. Interfaces are ideal for one-to-one or one-to-few commands where the caller wants to invoke behavior on a specific target.
Misconception check
Interfaces are not a replacement for all casts. If the caller needs proprietary data or methods only present on a single class, casting or a dedicated API may still be appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Interfaces declare messages so any implementing Blueprint can respond, keeping callers decoupled and flexible.

screens.title: Create a Blueprint Interface asset
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: declare messages that will be implemented later

narration.text: Creating a Blueprint Interface is a simple, repeatable process you will use often. In the Content Browser, right-click and choose Blueprints → Blueprint Interface. Name it with a clear prefix such as BPI_Interactable or BPI_LightSwitch so its intent is obvious. Open the asset and add functions for each message you need. Keep messages focused: a ToggleLight message might have no inputs, while Interact might accept a PlayerController reference. Remember interfaces only declare inputs and outputs. They do not hold logic or variables. That means you must design the message signature thoughtfully so implementers receive the context they need. A useful mnemonic is: Inputs carry context, outputs return results. After declaring functions, save the asset. You now have a contract ready to be implemented by Actors or Components. One common oversight is adding implementation logic to the wrong place; the interface never contains logic. If you find yourself adding behavior there, move it into the implementing Blueprint. Now you can add this interface to any Blueprint's Class Settings to implement the declared messages. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Create a Blueprint Interface asset
Create a Blueprint Interface asset
Step-by-step: declare messages that will be implemented later
Steps
  1. In Content Browser: right-click → Blueprints → Blueprint Interface. Give it a clear prefix like BPI_.
  2. Open the interface asset and Add New Function for each message you need.
  3. Design the function signature: add inputs for context, outputs for results. Keep them minimal.
  4. Save the asset. It now serves as a message contract other Blueprints can implement.
Design tip & example
Example: Create BPI_LightSwitch. Add ToggleLight with no inputs. For Interact patterns, include a PlayerController reference input so implementers know who asked for the interaction.
Misstep to avoid
Do not place implementation logic inside the interface asset. If you need shared helper code, use a shared function library or component, not the interface itself.
Mnemonic

Inputs carry context. Outputs return results. Interfaces only declare these pins.

screens.title: Implementing an interface on Actors and Components
screens.subtitle: Add the interface in Class Settings and create the implementation event

narration.text: Implementing an interface is a two-step workflow that lives inside the Blueprint you want to respond. First, open the Actor or Component Blueprint and navigate to Class Settings. Under Interfaces click Add and select your interface asset, such as BPI_LightSwitch. Once added, the interface functions appear in My Blueprint under an Interfaces section. Right-click the function and choose Implement Event or Implement Function to create the event graph node where you write behavior. For an Actor Light, implement ToggleLight to toggle the Point Light component's visibility or intensity. For a Component you might implement the same message to change a local state or trigger component behavior. A frequent mistake is forgetting to add the interface in Class Settings; if the function isn't visible under My Blueprint, you won't be able to implement it. Another useful note: interfaces can be implemented on components as well as Actors, letting you encapsulate behavior and reuse it across different owners. This pattern supports modular design and keeps logic localized. Implementing an interface on Actors and Components means add the interface in class settings, then implement event to provide the blueprint's concrete response to the message.. In practical terms, add the interface in class settings and create the implementation event. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Add the interface in Class Settings, then Implement Event to provide the Blueprint's concrete response to the message.

Implementing an interface on Actors and Components
Add the interface in Class Settings and create the implementation event
Steps to implement
  1. Open the target Blueprint and go to Class Settings.
  2. Under Interfaces click Add and select your BPI asset.
  3. In My Blueprint find Interfaces and right-click the function → Implement Event.
  4. Write the event graph logic to respond to the message for this specific Blueprint.
Example: BP_Light
Add BPI_LightSwitch, implement ToggleLight to toggle the Point Light component's visibility or intensity. The event executes when the player calls ToggleLight on the actor.
Common mistake
If you don't see the functions under My Blueprint, confirm the interface is added to Class Settings. Implementing without adding it is not possible.
Key Takeaway

Interfaces are added in Class Settings; implementing the event is how the Blueprint supplies its unique behavior.

screens.title: Call Interface Messages safely
screens.subtitle: Use Does Implement Interface before sending messages

narration.text: Calling an interface message is straightforward, but doing it safely is important for clear logic and easier debugging. When you have an object reference that might implement the interface, use Does Implement Interface with the object and the interface class. This node returns true if the object can respond. If true, call the message node such as Interact or ToggleLight on the same object reference. This pattern ensures you only attempt an action on objects that can handle it, avoiding silent misses that are hard to trace. For the player interact flow, perform a sphere overlap or line trace to collect nearby actors, iterate the results, run Does Implement Interface for each, and branch to call the message when true. A common error is calling the message without checking; the engine will ignore the call if the target lacks the interface, which can mislead you while debugging. Another tip: add a small print or log in the implemented event to confirm the call reached the target. This confirms both the Does Implement Interface check and the implementation are functioning. Call Interface Messages safely means trace/overlap → for each actor → does implement interface ? call message : skip. add logs to confirm execution.. In practical terms, use does implement interface before sending messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe call pattern
keyIdea.text: Trace/overlap → For Each Actor → Does Implement Interface ? Call message : skip. Add logs to confirm execution.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Call Interface Messages safely
Call Interface Messages safely
Use Does Implement Interface before sending messages
Pattern
Trace / Overlap → ForEach Actor → Does Implement Interface(BPI_X) → Branch → Call Message
This ensures that you only send the message to capable objects. The Does Implement Interface node acts like a capability check rather than an expensive cast chain.
Debug tip
Place a print string in the implemented event to see when the target responds. If the print doesn't appear, confirm the interface is added in Class Settings and the Does Implement Interface condition returned true.
Concrete example
Player performs Sphere Overlap Actors, loops results, uses Does Implement Interface with BPI_LightSwitch. If true, call ToggleLight on the actor to flip the light's visibility.
Key Takeaway

Always check Does Implement Interface before calling a message to avoid silent, hard-to-find failures.

screens.title: Player interact flow: Trace → Check → Call
screens.subtitle: Implement a robust player's Interact that works with many interactables

narration.text: A reliable player Interact flow combines spatial queries with interface checks. Start by adding a collision volume such as a sphere overlap or using a line trace from the camera to detect candidate actors. On the Interact input event, run a Sphere Overlap Actors with the player's location and a reasonable radius, collecting an array of potential targets. For each actor in the array, call Does Implement Interface with your BPI_Interactable or BPI_LightSwitch. If the check returns true, call the Interact or ToggleLight message on that actor and optionally break if you only want the nearest target to respond. This flow avoids casting to many classes and keeps the player's graph clean. A common misconception is that you must use only line traces; sphere overlap is often friendlier for close-range interactions and multiple nearby objects. For debug, visualize the overlap radius and add print statements to the implemented events. This pattern scales: adding new interactable types requires only implementing the interface on the new Blueprints, never changing the player logic. Player interact flow: Trace → Check → Call means sphere overlap → foreach actor → does implement interface? → call message. keep player logic ignorant of target classes.. In practical terms, implement a robust player's interact that works with many interactables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Sphere Overlap → ForEach Actor → Does Implement Interface? → Call message. Keep player logic ignorant of target classes.

Implement a robust player's Interact that works with many interactables
Example blueprint flow
// Input Action Interact (Pressed)
Input Action Interact (Pressed)
-> Sphere Overlap Actors (
   World Context: Self,
   Sphere Pos: GetActorLocation,
   Radius: 200.0,
   Out Actors: ForEachLoop)
-> ForEachLoop (Array Element: TargetActor)

This pattern keeps the player graph short and expressive. Use a break after calling if you only want a single target to respond.
Design choices
  • Use Sphere Overlap for short-range, multi-target interactions.
  • Use Line Trace for precise, aimed interactions.
  • Decide whether one or multiple targets should respond; use ForEach with optional break.
Key Takeaway

A short trace/check/call pattern keeps player logic stable while enabling any new implementer to respond without changes to the player blueprint.

screens.title: Interfaces across inheritance hierarchies
screens.subtitle: Use one interface for Actors and Components from different base classes

narration.text: One of the most powerful aspects of Blueprint Interfaces is that they ignore inheritance. An interface is not tied to a base class, so a BP_Door inheriting from Actor, a BP_Switch also an Actor, and a BP_InventoryComponent inheriting from ActorComponent can all implement the same BPI_Interactable. The caller does not care about their class lineage; it only checks whether the object implements the interface. This capability simplifies architecture when you want a shared contract across varied systems. A practical example: a ToggleLight message could be implemented by a BP_Light Actor to toggle a Point Light, and also by a LightComponent that manages light intensity. This reduces duplication and centralizes the interaction contract while allowing the implementer to decide how to act. A misconception is thinking interfaces replace inheritance; they complement it. Use inheritance for shared data and behavior among similar types, and interfaces for shared capabilities across different kinds of objects. This combination lets you design modular, extensible interactions across your project. Interfaces across inheritance hierarchies means interfaces let diverse classes implement the same capability without forcing a shared base class.. In practical terms, use one interface for actors and components from different base classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cross-hierarchy contracts
keyIdea.text: Interfaces let diverse classes implement the same capability without forcing a shared base class.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Interfaces across inheritance hierarchies
Interfaces across inheritance hierarchies
Use one interface for Actors and Components from different base classes
Why this matters
Interfaces are class-agnostic. They make it possible for unrelated types to promise the same behavior. This reduces the need for common base classes and lets you attach behavior where it makes sense—on Actors, Components, or even AI controllers.
Example
A BP_Light Actor and a LightComponent both implement ToggleLight. The player calls ToggleLight and both kinds of objects can respond appropriately without any casting logic.
Design advice
  • Use interfaces for capabilities shared across different systems.
  • Use inheritance for shared implementation and data among closely related classes.
  • Mix both: a base Actor can implement helper behavior while specific components implement the same interface for modularity.
Key Takeaway

Interfaces let you express capabilities across unrelated types, increasing architectural flexibility without forcing a shared base class.

screens.title: Interfaces vs Event Dispatchers vs Casting
screens.subtitle: Choose the right communication pattern for your use case

narration.text: Choosing among interfaces, event dispatchers, and casting depends on intent. Use casting when you require class-specific data or methods unavailable through a common contract. Casting exposes full type APIs, but at a maintenance cost: callers must know the callee's exact class. Use interfaces when you want to command a specific target to perform an action—one-to-one or one-to-few interactions. Interfaces define a clear contract and keep the caller ignorant of the implementer's class. Use Event Dispatchers when you need broadcasting: many listeners react to a single event. Dispatchers simplify broadcasting state changes but are less appropriate when you need to address a specific object and expect a direct command back. A common error is using a dispatcher for targeted commands; this complicates control flow and can make it hard to know which listener executed. In sum, ask: do you need a targeted command (interface), a broadcast notification (dispatcher), or access to class-specific APIs (cast)? That question will guide your architecture and keep communication clean and maintainable. Interfaces vs Event Dispatchers vs Casting means interfaces for targeted commands, dispatchers for broadcasting, and casting for class-specific api access.. In practical terms, choose the right communication pattern for your use case. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One-to-one commands. Define messages and let implementers decide how to respond. Best for targeted actions like Interact or ToggleLight.
Event Dispatchers
One-to-many notifications where many listeners should react to a single event. Good for global signals like OnLevelLoaded or OnPlayerDamaged broadcasting to systems.
Casting
Access class-specific APIs or data. Use when the caller legitimately needs the callee's unique methods or properties, but accept tighter coupling as a trade-off.
Decision reminder

Ask: targeted command, broadcast notification, or class-specific API? The answer determines interfaces, dispatchers, or casting respectively.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build the light switch interactable
screens.subtitle: Follow the chapter's light switch example step-by-step

narration.text: We'll walk through the light switch example from the chapter so you can implement it in your project. First create BPI_LightSwitch and add a ToggleLight function with no inputs. Next create BP_Light as an Actor, add a Static Mesh and Point Light component, and set the light's intensity to zero so it's initially off. In BP_Light's Class Settings add BPI_LightSwitch. In My Blueprint right-click ToggleLight → Implement Event. Inside the event, get the Point Light component, use Is Visible, invert that boolean, and feed it into Set Visibility for the Point Light. In your player character, add an interaction input and perform a Sphere Overlap Actors centered on the player with a small radius. For each actor hit call Does Implement Interface for BPI_LightSwitch, branch when true, and call ToggleLight on the target. Place instances of BP_Light in the level and test. This hands-on loop shows how creation, implementation, and calling combine into a flexible interactable system. Did the light toggle when you pressed interact? If not, confirm the interface is added to Class Settings and that your overlap found the actor.

screens.title: Debugging and common mistakes
screens.subtitle: Checks and tips when interface messages don't run as expected

narration.text: When interface messages don't trigger, a few recurring issues usually cause the problem. First, verify the interface is added to the target Blueprint's Class Settings. If it isn't, the function won't appear under My Blueprint and cannot be implemented. Second, confirm your Does Implement Interface check actually returned true; add a print before calling the message to see the branch outcome. Third, ensure the overlap or trace found the same actor instance placed in the level—don't confuse the class with a different spawned instance. Fourth, if the event executes but the behavior doesn't appear, check the implementation, for example that Set Visibility targets the correct Point Light component and not a differently named component. Fifth, remember that calling the message on an object that doesn't implement the interface silently does nothing, so explicit checks and logging are essential. As a pro-tip, add a small print in every implemented event that includes the actor's name; that immediate feedback reduces guesswork. Finally, if multiple targets respond unexpectedly, refine your overlap radius or stop after the first valid call. These checks make interface behavior reliable and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Confirm interface in Class Settings, Does Implement Interface returns true, trace/overlap found the expected actor, and component references are correct.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts you should retain. A Blueprint Interface is a declaration-only contract of messages that different Blueprints can implement to enable decoupled communication. An Interface Message is a declared function that can be called on any object implementing the interface. Decoupled communication means objects interact without needing to know each other's concrete types, which reduces coupling and improves extensibility. Use Does Implement Interface to check whether an object can respond to a message before calling it; this prevents silent misses and clarifies logic. Finally, Class Settings is where you add an interface to a Blueprint so the functions appear under My Blueprint and can be implemented. Keep these ideas handy when designing interaction systems so your player and interactables remain modular and easy to extend. narration.text: Keep three practical reminders as you apply interfaces. First, prefer interfaces when you need to command a specific object without tying the caller to concrete types. Second, always use Does Implement Interface before calling a message so your code clearly expresses intent and avoids silent failures. Third, use Class Settings to attach interfaces and then Implement Event to supply the actual behavior inside the Blueprint.
